title: Measurement of Length and Motion
description: Grade 6 Science: standard SI units, measuring length correctly, and types of motion — rectilinear, circular and periodic. Notes, solved examples and a practice test.

topics.title: Standard Units of Measurement (the SI System)
topics.concept:
To measure something is to compare it with a fixed amount and find how many times that amount it contains. Every measurement has two parts: a number and a unit (for example, ‘5 metres’ — 5 is the number, metre is the unit). Without the unit, the number has no meaning.

Long ago people measured length using body parts — the handspan, the cubit (elbow to fingertip) and the foot. The problem is that these differ from person to person, so the same wall might measure a different number of handspans for two people. To avoid confusion, the whole world agreed on fixed standard units that never change.

The accepted system is the SI system (from the French Système International). Its basic units include:

  • Length — the metre (m).
  • Mass — the kilogram (kg).
  • Time — the second (s).

Larger and smaller units are related to the metre in tens: 1 metre = 100 centimetres (cm); 1 centimetre = 10 millimetres (mm); and 1 kilometre (km) = 1000 metres. We choose a convenient unit for each job — kilometres for the distance between cities, metres for a room, centimetres for a book and millimetres for the thickness of a coin.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is the handspan not used as a standard unit of length?
examples.solution:
A standard unit must be the same for everyone.

  • The handspan differs from person to person.
  • So the same object would give different measurements, causing confusion.
examples.answer: Because a handspan is different for different people, it does not give the same measurement, so it cannot be a standard unit.

examples.problem: Example 2: Convert (a) 3 metres into centimetres and (b) 2000 metres into kilometres.
examples.solution:
Use 1 m = 100 cm and 1 km = 1000 m.

  • (a) 3 m = 3 × 100 = 300 cm.
  • (b) 2000 m = 2000 ÷ 1000 = 2 km.

examples.problem: Example 3: Which unit would you use to measure (a) the distance between two cities and (b) the thickness of a coin?
examples.solution:
Choose a unit that gives a convenient number.

  • (a) A large distance → kilometre (km).
  • (b) A very small length → millimetre (mm).

recap:
• A measurement has a number and a unit; the unit gives it meaning.
  • Body-part units (handspan, cubit, foot) vary, so we use fixed standard units.
  • The SI units: length = metre (m), mass = kilogram (kg), time = second (s).
  • 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 km = 1000 m; choose a convenient unit for each job.

quiz.q: Every measurement must have a number and a:
quiz.explanation: A measurement is meaningless without a unit.

quiz.q: The SI unit of length is the:
quiz.explanation: The metre is the SI unit of length.

topics.title: Methods for Measuring Length
topics.concept:
The most common tool for measuring length is a ruler (scale); a longer flexible measuring tape is used for bigger lengths like a room or a person’s height. To get a correct reading, we must use these tools carefully. There are three important rules.

  • Place the scale correctly. Lay the scale along the object touching it. Many rulers are worn at the zero end, so start measuring from the 0 mark (or any full mark) rather than the very edge.
  • Take the reading from the right position. If the object does not begin at 0, the length = (reading at the other end) − (reading at the start). For example, if an object lies between the 2 cm and 7 cm marks, its length is 7 − 2 = 5 cm.
  • Keep your eye in the correct position. Look at the mark straight on, directly above the point being read. If you look from an angle, you read a wrong value — an error called parallax error.

Some objects are not straight. To measure a curved line, lay a thread along the curve, mark where it begins and ends, then straighten the thread against a ruler. To measure the length of a curved or large object fairly, always use a suitable tool and these careful steps.

examples.problem: Example 1: An object is placed on a ruler with one end at the 2 cm mark and the other at the 9 cm mark. What is its length?
examples.solution:
When the object does not start at 0, subtract the readings.

  • Length = 9 cm − 2 cm.
  • Length = 7 cm.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is parallax error and how do we avoid it?
examples.solution:
Parallax error comes from the position of the eye.

  • It is the wrong reading you get when you look at the scale from an angle.
  • Avoid it by keeping your eye directly above (straight in line with) the mark.
examples.answer: Parallax error is a wrong reading caused by viewing the scale from an angle; avoid it by looking straight down over the mark.

examples.problem: Example 3: How would you measure the length of a curved line drawn on paper?
examples.solution:
A straight ruler cannot follow a curve directly.

  • Lay a thread carefully along the curved line.
  • Mark the start and end on the thread, then straighten it against a ruler to read the length.
examples.answer: Place a thread along the curve, mark its length, then measure the straightened thread with a ruler.

recap:
• Use a ruler for small lengths and a measuring tape for larger ones.
  • Place the scale touching the object; if it does not start at 0, length = end reading − start reading.
  • Keep the eye straight above the mark to avoid parallax error.
  • Measure a curved line using a thread, then straighten it against a ruler.

quiz.q: An object lies between the 3 cm and 11 cm marks on a ruler. Its length is:
quiz.explanation: Length = 11 - 3 = 8 cm when the object does not start at 0.

quiz.q: The wrong reading caused by looking at a scale from an angle is called:
quiz.explanation: Viewing a scale from an angle gives a parallax error.

topics.title: Types of Motion
topics.concept:
An object is said to be in motion when its position changes with time compared to a fixed point around it. If its position does not change, it is at rest. Whether something is moving is judged with respect to its surroundings — a tree is at rest with respect to the ground, but appears to move when you watch it from a running train.

Motion is of several kinds, and an object may show more than one at a time:

  • Rectilinear (straight-line) motion — movement along a straight line. Examples: a car on a straight road, a falling stone, a marching soldier.
  • Circular motion — movement along a circular path. Examples: the hands of a clock, a stone tied to a string and whirled, the blades of a fan.
  • Periodic (or oscillatory) motion — movement that repeats after equal intervals of time. Examples: a swinging pendulum, a child on a swing, the vibrating string of a guitar.

Some everyday motions combine types. The wheel of a moving bicycle rotates (circular motion) while the bicycle as a whole moves forward in a straight line (rectilinear motion). Recognising the type of motion helps us describe and study how things move.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the type of motion shown by (a) the hands of a clock and (b) a stone falling straight down.
examples.solution:
Match the path to the type of motion.

  • (a) Clock hands move along a circle → circular motion.
  • (b) A falling stone moves in a straight line → rectilinear motion.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why is the motion of a swinging pendulum called periodic?
examples.solution:
Periodic motion repeats at equal time intervals.

  • The pendulum swings to and fro.
  • It returns to the same position after equal time gaps, so the motion repeats.
examples.answer: Because it swings to and fro and repeats its movement after equal intervals of time.

examples.problem: Example 3: A moving bicycle shows two kinds of motion at once. Name them.
examples.solution:
Look at the wheel and the bicycle as a whole.

  • The wheel turns round and round → circular motion.
  • The whole bicycle moves forward in a line → rectilinear motion.
examples.answer: The wheel shows circular motion while the whole bicycle shows rectilinear (straight-line) motion.

recap:
• An object is in motion when its position changes with time relative to its surroundings; otherwise it is at rest.
  • Rectilinear motion is along a straight line (a falling stone).
  • Circular motion is along a circular path (clock hands, a fan).
  • Periodic motion repeats after equal time intervals (a pendulum).

quiz.q: The motion of a stone falling straight down is:
quiz.explanation: Movement along a straight line is rectilinear motion.

quiz.q: A swinging pendulum that repeats its movement at equal time intervals shows ___ motion.
quiz.explanation: Motion that repeats after equal intervals of time is periodic motion.

questions.q: To measure a quantity means to compare it with a fixed:
questions.explanation: Measuring compares a quantity with a fixed amount, the unit.

questions.q: Every measurement is written as a number together with a:
questions.explanation: A measurement needs both a number and a unit.

questions.q: Body parts like the handspan are not used as standard units because they:
questions.explanation: Body-part lengths vary between people, so they are not reliable standards.

questions.q: The SI unit of length is the:
questions.explanation: The metre is the SI unit of length.

questions.q: How many centimetres are there in 1 metre?
questions.explanation: 1 metre = 100 centimetres.

questions.q: 1 kilometre is equal to:
questions.explanation: 1 kilometre = 1000 metres.

questions.q: The best unit to measure the thickness of a coin is the:
questions.explanation: A coin is very thin, so the millimetre is suitable.

questions.q: An object lies between the 4 cm and 10 cm marks of a ruler. Its length is:
questions.explanation: Length = 10 - 4 = 6 cm.

questions.q: While reading a scale, your eye should be:
questions.explanation: Looking straight above the mark avoids parallax error.

questions.q: A wrong reading caused by viewing the scale from an angle is called:
questions.explanation: Viewing from an angle causes a parallax error.

questions.q: A curved line is best measured using a:
questions.explanation: Lay a thread along the curve, then straighten it against a ruler.

questions.q: An object is in motion when its ___ changes with time.
questions.explanation: Motion means a change of position with time.

questions.q: The motion of the hands of a clock is an example of:
questions.explanation: Clock hands move along a circular path.

questions.q: Motion that repeats after equal intervals of time is called:
questions.explanation: Periodic motion repeats at equal time intervals, like a pendulum.

questions.q: A car moving on a straight road shows ___ motion.
questions.explanation: Movement along a straight road is rectilinear motion.

questions.q: Two friends measure the same desk in handspans and get different numbers. This best shows the need for:
questions.explanation: Different results from body-part units show why fixed standard units are needed.

questions.q: A pencil reads 1 cm at one end and 16 cm at the other on a worn ruler. Its true length is:
questions.explanation: Length = 16 - 1 = 15 cm; subtract the readings when not starting at 0.

questions.q: A child on a swing and a vibrating guitar string are both examples of:
questions.explanation: Both repeat their movement at equal intervals, so they show periodic motion.

questions.q: The wheel of a moving cart shows circular motion, while the cart moves forward. This shows an object can have:
options: More than one type of motion at once
questions.explanation: The turning wheel (circular) and the forward-moving cart (rectilinear) happen together.

questions.q: A tree appears to move backward when seen from a moving train because motion is judged with respect to:
questions.explanation: Motion is always relative to a chosen reference point or the surroundings.

questions.q: To measure the distance walked along a winding garden path, the most suitable method is to use a:
options: Short straight ruler held in the air
Thread or flexible tape laid along the path
questions.explanation: A flexible thread or measuring tape follows the curve, which a stiff ruler cannot.
